speechtext: That that portion of the 49th rule which limits the time for presenting private Bills be suspended in reference to the Bill respecting the Subsidiary High Court of the Ancient Order of Foresters of the Dominion of Canada, in accordance with the recommendation contained in the 11th report of the Select Standing Committee on Standing Orders.

Before that motion is put, I wish to draw to the attention of the right hon. First Minister the frequency with which the rule with regard to private Bills is asked to be suspended. Earlier this session I drew his attention to the same thing, and I understood him to say that the first session of the new parliament was the proper time for the House to put its foot down on this growing practice, which tends to lengthen the session. Although we must he drawing measurably near the end of the session, the same disposition to suspend the rule continues. It is an evil that should be stopped, and I hope the government will exercise some reasonable control in the matter.

I wish to state that the urgency of this particular Bill was mentioned at the time permission was given to present the preliminary petition. It is the only Bill at all likely to infringe the rule of the House. It is of great importance that it should be passed this session. It is exactly similar in its terms to another Bill in regard to another society which was passed a week or two ago, and I trust the hon. gentleman will not insist on his objection.

I agree altogether with the sentiments expressed by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) ; but, we considered this particular case a few days ago, and came to the conclusion that the rule
ought to be allowed to stand aside with respect to this Bill, but with respect to this Bill alone-nothing else.

I observe there is a note at the end of this resolution stating that since then the yard-master has been removed to another sphere of duty and that his successor has been

appointed. Now, in order not to take up the time of the committee unnecessarily, I will submit to the hon. gentleman at the same time a resolution which was passed by the city council with respect to the expropriation of land on Upper Water street. The hon. gentleman, of course, is familiar with the line which connects the main line of the Intercolonial Railway with the deep water terminus ; he knows that part of Upper Water street In the city of Halifax is occupied by that line. It has been there for a great many years, I believe it was originally put there on account of the desire of the city to secure a terminus at deep water. They passed a resolution, as I understand, authorizing the laying of the railway on that portion, or a portion, of the street. The result of placing the railway there has been to narrow the street, of course, to a great extent, rendering it much less useful as a public highway than it was before. But that has not been the only result. A further result has been that the property immediately adjoining that on the west has been almost entirely destroyed for the purpose for which it was formerly used. It has deteriorated in value to an enormous extent.
Is that deterioration of recent occurrence ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I think it has been going on ever since the railway has been placed on the street, and the proprietors at one time commenced an action against the government for the purpose of recovering damages. The hon. gentleman knows the difficulty that arises where no portion of the proprietors' land has been taken. No portion of the land of any of these proprietors had been taken, and upon commencing litigation they found that there were great difficulties in1 succeeding, and eventually I think the petitions of right were not successful. Nevertheless, no one can doubt that these people have sustained great damage, and it would seem an equitable thing at least that some compensation should be made to them. Neither the former government nor this government could ever see their way clear to do anything, thinking that as there was no legal liability it was not an occasion that called for interference. Now, what the city council suggests in their resolution, which I will read, is that increased accommodation is required for the Intercolonial Railway at Halifax, both at the deep water terminus at North street, and at Richmond, and that the increased accommodation could be best provided by expropriating land between Water street and Lockman street, as far south as the deep water terminus. I believe the property could be acquired at a very reasonable rate, and I venture to think that the suggestion made by the city council in this resolution is worthy of very careful and earnest consideration on the part of the Minister of Railways and Canals and of the government. The matter arose in the city of Halifax recently in this way : It was proposed to erect a cold storage plant in the northern part of the city, and there was necessity in that connection to obtain a siding or some right of way over that portion of the Intercolonial Railway which runs along this street, and an application was made to the city council. In dealing with that, the city council passed this resolution :
With reference to the granting of permission for the laying of a railway siding on Upper Water street, that such permission could not he granted. Your committee would recommend, however, that immediate steps should be taken by the council to impress upon the Dominion government, not only the great desirability, from a commercial standpoint, but the utter necessity of the taking over of the land by the government in order to furnish anything like adequate facilities for the handling of freight.
That has since been followed up by another resolution of the council in the month of March, which is of the same purport, and I will not trouble the committee by reading it. I think the minister has already had this matter under consideration to some extent. I desire to press its importance upon him, not because it is a matter affecting my own city and my own constituency, but because it is a matter affecting the entire business of the Intercolonial Railway which comes into the city of Halifax. I think we may look for some development of that business, and I believe the minister himself looks for great development of business over the Intercolonial Railway into that city ; but as long as we do not have first-class accommodation and proper facilities for handling freight it would be impossible for that business to develop to any great degree. At the present time those who are more capable of forming an opinion upon this matter than I am, think that the facilities are not adequate to a proper development within a few years ; indeed they say the facilities are not sufficient for the business now. If that be so. it is necessary to provide increased facilities, and I see no better way in which the minister could do it than by taking that portion of land. In saying that, of course, I speak with great diffidence, because I am well aware that I have no practical knowledge of the subject which will entitle my opinion to much respect. But it does seem to me that the land lying immediately beside the track of the Intercolonial Railway, extending from the North street station down to the deep water terminus, is land that could be more useful to the Intercolonial Railway for the purpose referred to than any other land that I am aware of in that vicinity.

Mr. Chairman, having reference, in the first place, to what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has stated, particularly in regard to taking over the property on Water street, I may say to my hon. friend that that subject has received a good deal of consideration from the department and from myself personally. I have not, however, I am free to confess, up to the present moment, felt that the interest of the railway or the public service was so much involved in the question as the interest of the private land-owners themselves. They naturally have a desire to dispose of this property, property which I agree, has been, to some extent, possibly to a considerable extent, depreciated in value by reason of the railway line running along that street. But, this is not, by any means, a recent grievance, it is one of very long standing. The condition which exists today has prevailed for many years. I do not think that things are much worse at this moment than they were ten, or fifteen, or twenty years ago ; so that, while I think that if we had plenty of money, if things were easy with us, it would be rather an advantage for the railway to own this particular property, we have not thought that, in the pressure under which we were to afford the accommodation to the public, we ought to defer doing what is altogether and entirely necessary in the public interest, doing what is more for a private than a public interest, or which is as much a private as it is a public interest. My hon. friend, when he suggested that this property would be a good property for us to acquire in order to improve our facilities, did not have in his mind the consideration that it is not always best that a railway should acquire property for such a purpose in the heart of the city or necessarily very close to the city. The object of railway policy in that direction at the present time is rather to get out of a city, to go where you can get land as cheaply as possible, and where you can lay down your yards at the least possible expense. We are endeavouring to do that, and that is why we are doing what we are at Richmond and in the neighbourhood of the North street station, rather than in the more settled part nearer the centre of the city. We have endeavoured to meet the urgent demands of the business people of Halifax in our present proposals. I do not say that we have covered all the ground that we would desire to cover, but we are approaching the question with a full appreciation of the necessity of more and improved accommodation being provided for the business of Halifax. It is unquestionably growing, it has grown of late, there is a congestion at the present time, and business men have good reason to complain that they have not the facilities provided for them that they Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
need. We think that what we are now proposing to do will very largely meet the present needs at all events, and meet the needs of the immediate future as well. I think if my hon. friend understands, as I am quite sure he does, what our scheme of improvement is, he will admit that we are responding reasonably, at all events, to the demand which the business men of Halifax have made upon us ; at all events, in an equal degree with any other portion of the country through which the line runs. My hon. friend read in the resolutions that it was the opinion of the Board of Trade and the city council of Halifax that the line should be double tracked between Halifax and Windsor Junction. That question has been looked into. We have not come to a final decision in respect to it. It will be an expensive work when it is undertaken, and my own desire has been rather that we should see whether or not, for the present, and for some few years to come, we might not extend our sidings. We might lay a double track for a few miles of the distance between these two points, laying it down where it could be built less expensively and thereby answer the purposes of the relief to traffic. To double track tlfe whole line between Halifax and Windsor Junction would be an expensive work, because there are points where a good deal of heavy rock cutting would have to be done. I think we can have six or eight miles of track in one continuous line on a portion of the road which would be comparatively inexpensive, and which would afford very great relief and sufficient relief to answer for some time. It is to that point that we are now directing attention. I think I would like, before deciding upon it in my own mind and before dealing with the conflicting views which may obtain upon it, to look over that section of the road myself, which' I think I will be able to do at the close of the session. During this session, at all events, I would not be in a position to ask my colleagues to make any appropriation for the purpose of laying down either all or any portion of the double track between these two points.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blair) perhaps, misunderstood the ground upon which I was putting forth the suggestion that the property on Upper Water street should be acquired by the government for the purposes of the Intercolonial Railway. My reference to the depreciation of the property of the landowners there, was more with the view of pointing out to the minister that the property could be acquired at a very cheap rate. I did not intend to suggest, that, because these gentlemen had certainly what one might call a moral grievance on account of the depreciation, therefore, we should acquire the property. I was not suggesting

that, but I was pointing out that it could be acquired at a very low figure. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals says that this is not necessary, and that what is being done at Richmond, will answer the purpose for the present. Of course, he knows a great deal more about the actual working of the railway than I can pretend to know, but I do understand that at deep water itself there is a very great deal of difficulty on account of the lack of room for sending cars there, loading and unloading them, and a lack of facilities for the purpose of handling the business of the Intercolonial Railway. I do not know to what extent that can be remedied by having a yard at Richmond a mile off or more. It did seem to me that this land which is immediately adjoining would improve the accommodation which needs to be improved at deep water, and I have no doubt it would. Of course, the question remains as to whether the necessity is great enough to justify the hon. minister in going to the expense of acquiring the land. The hon. gentleman is responsible for any opinion in regard to it, and of course he is in a better position than 1 am to form an opinion in regard to it. But, I do know that a great many people and the leading business men of Halifax think it is absolutely necessary now, or in the immediate future, to increase the room at the deep water terminus itself, or in its immediate vicinity. I trust, that, although the hon. minister may not see his way clear to take that into consideration now, he will bear it in mind and that if the accommodation is necessary for the proper development of the business of the Intercolonial Railway at Halifax it may not be delayed to a too distant future.

It is connected with the improvement of the deep water terminus.

speechtext:
In connection with these appropriations for the Railway Department,
I wish for a moment to again direct the attention of the minister and of the government to the fact that the time has come when the government system of railways* should be administered absolutely independent of politics. If we ever are to have a national system of railways in this country, we must begin by taking our present system out of politics. I trust that before this parliament meets again the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) and the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock) will be able to announce with the sanction of the government that hereafter the railways and tire post office are to be conducted irrespective of all kinds of political influences; that the administration of the railway will be in the hands of the best officials that can be obtained, that they will be well jraid. and that they can do their work unhampered by political interference. The idea of national railways is growing in Canada, and I want to see it grow. I want to see the Intercolonial Railway extended from ocean to ocean. I am prepared to see the Intercolonial Railway extended to the Georgian Bay to-day if a reasonable proposition for that purpose can be secured. To begin with, let us do as they do in England, and take the administration of our railways outside of politics. No member of parliament should have a word to say in the appointment of postmasters or brakesmen or anything of that kind.
You used to have a lot to say about it.

The gentlemen who sit on the other side of the House think this is an absurd doctrine. They like to be dabbling- in this kind of business, and they like to be trafficking- in senatorships. If that kind of traffic has obtained in the past the people of Canada want to see it ended now and for ever.
We like to follow your good example.
I hope the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan,) who represents the cakewalk district of this country will follow a good example when he gets it from a man like me.

Oh, oh.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

We have had enough of cake-walk interruptions in this House, and I hope we have heard the last of them. Now-, Mr. Chairman, I do trust that the Minister of Railways and the First Minister will recognize that Canada is proud of her national railway, and that the people of this country wuuid like to see it developed. I believe that the people of Canada would like to see the railways and the telegraph and telephone systems taken over by the government, but to begin with we must take these enterprises outside the domain of politics. I hope the Conservative party will come before the country in a very short time and declare that it is one of the planks in their platform to de-politicalize the railway system and the post office service of this country. If that be done, the people will think more and more of these great public institutions, and will be prepared to invest more of their money in the extension of them.

We have had an appropriation for the subway, and have expended it.
