speechtext: And this is to pay for the land you take ?

This is to pay for the land we have been obliged to take, and land damages. The chief engineer reports that this amount, he believes, will be sufficient to cover both. Last year or the year before we had an estimate, speaking from memory,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: of between $10,000 or $12,000 for the work, which has been done.

This is a small item, but it is an extraordinary statement the minister makes. There was apparently a level crossing, and for the purpose of protecting the public he builds a subway. How could damages to the extent of $1,000, or any damages, occur ?
They certainly occurred in Toronto, when a subway was built there on the streets.
This is a subway on an ordinary road in the country. What land damages could occur two or three miles outside of Amherst, for which $1,000 would be payable ?

We are not going to pay any more than we are obliged to pay. The names of the claimants are Charles Patterson and the heirs of Moffat. In making this subway, I understand that we have cut into and injured the land of these two people. This roadway goes down a valley, and then rises up and crosses the railway on a level crossing, and we are building a subway under the tracks, and in doing so we are cutting into the valley on the one side or the other beyond our own boundaries.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How far is this place from Amherst ?
About a quarter of a mile.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What quantity of ground is taken ?
I do not know how much.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would like to ask the minister in regard to the accommodation at Sydney. I am requested to ask if he has come to any settled conclusion as to whether he will make any change in regard to the running of trains to North Sydney and Sydney. As I understand, North Sydney is on the main line, while Sydney is on a branch.

The hon. gentleman was not here when I made my reply on that subject, but he will find it in ' Hansard,' to the effect that we will be issuing the timetable for the coming season in a short time, and we contemplate making arrangements to remove the dissatisfaction which exists, which has existed for many years, but which is undoubtedly becoming more acute by reason of the increased business at Sydney. WTe hope to provide such accommodation for both places as will satisfy the rea-

sonable demands of the people resident in those places.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: By what means do you hope to accomplish that ?

There would be different means of accomplishing it. One would be by having a train run out from North Sydney, and connect with the express when it arrives at Sydney junction-the main express going into Sydney, which would, perhaps, carry the major part of the travel. Another arrangement that might be made would be to increase the number of our express trains from Mulgrave, and arrange to have one train a day leaving North Sydney, and one train a day leaving Sydney, and on the return one train going to North Sydney and the other to Sydney. I do not know that it would be expedient for me at this moment to state to which of these plans my own preference would incline. But, the hon. gentleman can say to those who are inquiring of him, that the subject is not being overlooked, but that it will be dealt with in a manner which I am sure will be reasonably satisfactory to the people.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
My information is, that the first plan would not be satisfactory, for this reason, that it would be making practically a branch of what was originally a main line. It would necessitate a transfer at Sydney Junction, instead of the train going on to North Sydney, which, I am told, is practically on the main line, and connects with the regular boat, which carries a large number of passengers. If the other plan were carried out, of running through trains-one from North Sydney and another from Sydney

I do not suppose that the same objection would prevail. But, the first suggestion will not, so far as I am informed, meet with the approval of the people of North Sydney at all. They have protested against that before, and will likely do so again.

I do not expect to be able to satisfy the people of both points, and I have some doubts as to whether I shall be able to satisfy them at either of the points. If the last suggestion I made were to be adopted, I am quite sure that the people, at least from one of these localities, would complain that both trains were not serving their particular point. There are objections to the running of through trains unless the .needs of business justify it, and it is not a serious consideration for people to get on board a day car-a comfortable commodious car-and run up five or six miles and then change into another car. That is not at all a serious grievance, and if they can get first-class service, as they will by submitting to a little inconvenience of that kind, I do not think they can make much of a
case on which to appeal to the public against the decision of the department. We have been giving the people of Cape Breton a great deal better service than they have been heretofore receiving. We have put additional trains on, and I think we will be justified in still more improving the service by giving, probably all the year round, a day and night service each way. But for some little time to come, it would not be reasonable to ask us to duplicate that improved service for both towns.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It may not be much trouble for passengers to get on and off a train, but when it is contemplated to make what was heretofore the main line a branch line, and make the other the main line, it seems to me it would be wise first to determine which line carries the largest number of passengers and the greater amount of freight. I understand that North Sydney is the line which connects with the boat line, whereas the other does not connect with any regular boat line.

The proportion of passenger and freight traffic is very much larger to Sydney than North Sydney. I would think two or three times as large. The other has steamboat connection with the Bruce and Newfoundland line, but with all that there is no real analogy between the two cases, so far as the volume of passenger and freight traffic is concerned. When you get to North Sydney you get practically to the terminus of railway connection, except so far as steamers are concerned, but when you get to Sydney you have connection with the Louisburg railway, along which line there are several important mines and large centres of population. The mines of the Dominion Coal Company are located chiefly along that railway, and the connection with Sydney brings you into contact with the population at these mines and at other points on the Louisburg railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What would be the respective population of the two places 7
The population of Sydney is about half as much again as that of North Sydney, and in addition you are serving the population of these mining towns and villages along the Louisburg line.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Has the hon. minister sufficient terminals at Sydney or is he likely to have to buy terminals at a high price from real estate speculators 7 I hope that the country has something to show for the $2,000,000 invested in terminals at Halifax. The esplanade at Toronto is a very valuable work, which cost a great deal of money and is traversed by miles of track, but I do not think it cost quite $2,000,000.	$2,-
000,000 for terminal facilities in Halifax is

rather a large item, and I would like to know whether the people are getting value for their money. If North Sydney is to develop as we are told it will, I hope that the hon. gentleman will have proper terminal facilities there, and thus avoid the necessity of having to pay two or three years hence, exaggerated prices for real estate in that town.
Original construction, $2,000.
Is that for land damages ?

No, this is construction, the old item.
Land Damages-Oxford and New Glasgow and Cape Breton division of the Intercolonial Railway, $1,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This is an old item. Usually for the last ten or twelve years, $2,000 has been voted, but this year we believe that $1,000 will be sufficient. The only claims now pending relate to the Cape Breton division. They are : Charles E. Leonard. land damage in connection with the right of way [DOT] of the original construction of the Cape Breton line ; Catherine McKenzie, and James and David Dowling, for the diversion of a stream. We believe that the amount here asked for will be sufficient for the claims to be paid during the year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We might as well take up the first item, which was held oversteel rails and fastenings.

Very well.
Railways and Canals-Chargeable to Capital- Railways-Intercolonial Railway-Steel rails and fastenings, $500,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I see by the returns brought down by the minister that he had tenders from seven parties, and as he stated, they were very nearly the same as that at which the contract was given. Did the hon. gentleman make inquiries as to the price of rails in the open market, the price paid by the ordinary railways of the country ?
To what time does the hon. gentleman refer ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Within the last eight or nine months. The price has not varied for about six months.
I think the price to-day is lower. If you are ready to place an order to-day for delivery nine or twelve months hence, you can get quite a reduction upon the price we had to pay last year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What is the price now ?
I do not know, but I think that it is probably $5 or $6 less than it was.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The price is $24 a ton.

The highest market price at any time during the last five months has been $25 a ton. I have here the contract that the hon. minister has made with Mr. Clergue and his company, and I must say it is the most extraordinary contract that I have ever known to be presented to a House of parliament.	This
agreement was made in October, 1900, one month before the general election. I gathered from what the minister said the other day that he was ashamed of it, because he stated that it was for only 25,000 tons of steel.
No, I stated just what it was, did I not ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
This contract is for
125,000	tons of steel. That is to say, here is a contract for about $4,000,000 that the Minister of Railways and Canals has entered into without consulting parliament and without a single dollar voted by parliament. What becomes of the promises made by these hon. gentlemen when in opposition ? What becomes of the principle they promised to carry out if returned to power-that no contract of any importance would be given without being first submitted to the House for its sanction ? Here the hon. minister, off his own bat, a month before the election, enters into a contract with a man who has had not a single forge, who was not in a position to manufacture a single steel rail, for 125,000 tons of rails at a price for the first year of $32.60, the price afterwards to be fixed in a very uncertain manner. Here are the words of the contract:
Whereas, for the purpose of encouraging the erection and equipment in Canada of plant and machinery for the manufacture and production on the most modern principle, of steel rails and plates and bridge material, the aforementioned Minister of Railways and Canals has been authorized to execute a contract guaranteeing to the company the acceptance by Her Majesty, during the five years next following, of 25,000 tons of steel rails at prices fixed as hereinafter specified. It is, therefore, agreed by and between Her Majesty, for herself, her successors and assigns, and the company for itself, its successors and assigns, that Her Majesty will in each year from the year 1901 to the year 1905, both inclusive, purchase from the company and take delivery of 25,000 tons of 2,240 pounds to the ton, of first quality steel rails, eighty pounds to the yard, of section from time totime prescribed and approved by the said minister.
Then, as to the price, it is fixed in this manner :
That, with the exception of the year 1901, for which year the price per ton is hereby fixed at

$32.60, the price for such rails per ton shall be the same as the pries obtainable for the same quality of rails in the open market in Great Britain at the time when the respective orders for such rails are given under the said contract.
Now, if the minister is correct-though I see nothing about it in his contract-there is from 2 to 3 per cent of nickel in the rails. Unless the nickel is mixed in England to get rails of the same quality, it will be impossible to fix the price by the market price of rails in England. The contractor, before he goes into the enterprise, has $3 per ton promised to him in the form of a bounty for every ton of steel manufactured in Canada.
He gets $3 per ton for pig iron and $3 per ton for steel.
And something out of the Ontario government.

Yes, he gets $G per ton from this government besides a bounty from the Ontario government. And he has a contract for five years to sell steel rails to a total of 25,000 tons, virtually at the price of $32.60 per ton. What better thing could a man desire with which to go into the market and raise capital for the purpose of fulfilling his contract ? The government have not only made an agreement for the purchase of these rails, but they have virtually furnished the capital to carry out the contract. I protest against this growing habit on the part of the government of letting contracts without tender. It was one of the principles laid down by these hon. gentlemen when they were in opposition that no contract should be let without tender. They also insisted that no contract of importance should be let without being first laid upon the Table of this House for the approval of parliament. I do not know what this country is coming to, when the purchase of locomotives, the purchase of cars, the enormous expenditure on capital account of nearly $2,000,000 for the Intercolonial is left to an individual, when it is left to the government of the country to enter into contracts for such enormous sums without competition. There is something wrong on the face of it. The contract does not bear the date it was entered into, it only says : ' An agreement made this day, 1900.' The party who engrossed and backed it was more honest than the party who copied the agreement, because he says the date of the agreement was in October, 1900.
Look at the agreement, I think you will see the date mentioned.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Oh, yes, 9th of October, 1900.
Was that the date the writs were issued for the elections ?

Very near it.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND * CANALS. It is difficult to follow the hon. gentleman in his statements, they are so wild, so misleading, so entirely inaccurate, so unfair. I confess I feel some difficulty in dealing with the statements as they merit. I am willing that a comparison should be made between the methods of this government and the methods of the government with which the hon. gentleman was connected. I am willing that the bona fides of the transaction should be sifted, and examined, and investigated, and turned over in every shape and form. And after you have done that, what will you find ? You will find simply that the government has endeavoured to pursue a course which, without a loss of a dollar to the public exchequer, would guarantee, if it were possible to do so, the establishment of an industry which will be of an enormous advantage to this country. I would not have expected that an hon. gentleman who belongs to a party that professes to absorb almost all interest in the industrial enterprises of Canada, should have been the first to complain of an arrangement of this kind, so well calculated to confer immense benefits upon the country, by the encouragement of an industry which could not possibly hope to succeed unless it received aid and encouragement in a proper and legitimate way from the government of the country. Now, Sir, away back in the month of June last, as I told the House yesterday, this subject was a matter of discussion. Before the close of the last session of parliament, I find, as early as the month of June, a formal proposal was made to the government by Mr. Clergue. If that proposal was one which was proper and commended itself to the approbation of the government, do I understand from the hon. gentleman that it ought to be rejected because an election might possibly occur in the near future ? Do I understand the hon. gentleman to tell this House calmly and seriously that that is the course which he and his party pursued when they were in power, that they abstained from entering into a proper, necessary and legitimate contract because somebody would suspect and charge them with having done so in view of an impending election ? I say it is childish and absurd ; and however much the hon. gentleman may have succeeded in warming himself up on this question, he will find it difficult to impress that view upon any reasonable electorate in any constituency in Canada. In the month of June, I say, we received a formal proposal from Mr. Clergue pointing out that they were anxious, in connectiou with their enterprises at the Soo, having large mineral interests, having an enormously valuable deposit of iron ore of a character which would make a superior steel, to establish an industry for making



rails in Canada. Well, will anybody say that is not a desirable thing to encourage ?
The Liberal party have said it from time to time.

I do not care what the Liberal party said. I do not think the Liberal party ever proclaimed any such policy. I think the hon. gentleman will find it difficult to quote even individual members of the Liberal party-and individual members are not competent to speak for the party-who declared themselves against any such proposition. As long as there is no wrong done to the country, as long as there is not a dollar of burden placed upon the exchequer beyond what is necessary and reasonable, as long as yon are not taking money out of the pockets of one person in order to put it into the pockets of another, I say it would be a laudable and legitimate policy and one which it is the bounden duty of any government to adopt and carry into operation, if they could do so under the circumstances which existed in this case. Mr. Clergue made this proposition, made it in good faith. It was considered in good faith, and it was finally determined upon by the government, not in the form of an order in council, hut some time before the order in council was passed, some time before the date of the contract. It was determined upon by the government, and the conditions upon which such contract would be made were settled by the government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When did the minister say the order in council was passed ?
If my memory serves me, it was in the month of September, not long before the date of the contract which has been read by the bon. gentleman.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The contract itself stares that the order in council was dated the 9th of October.

That may be the date on which the order was passed, but the recommendation to council, I am quite sure, went in in September, because I was not here on the 9th of October, and could not have been present at that time. ' On a memorandum dated the 26th of September.' Then the order goes on to say it was in September that the report went to council, and the order passed on the 9th October. Well, now, what are the terms of that contract ? If that is open to criticism, then let the hon. gentleman criticise it, as it is his right to do. Do the terms state that we are to pay to this Lake Superior Power Company any price they may ask ? Are we to pay a price higher than the market price? No, we are not to pay a price higher than the market price.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You are paying it this year.

We are not paying a price higher than the market price. If, six months, or nine months, or a year, after a contract has been made, the price has declined, it is not fair to any government, it is not fair to any individual, to say that he was paying an exorbitant price, and attempt to prove it by the fact that the price has since declined. That is no evidence. At the time this contract was made the price of rails, from what information I could gather, was as high in the English market as the price we paid.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Was it necessary for the hon. gentleman to enter into such a contract at the time be did, and pay the exorbitant price that he now admits be paid for these rails ? Did he require the rails then ?
I want the hon. gentleman to understand that he is not quoting my observations correctly in the remotest degree when he says that I admitted paying an exorbitant price.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why, the hon. gentleman said a moment ago that the rails could be bought probably $6 a ton cheaper now than then.

But what does that prove? Does it prove that when the contract was made the price was higher than the market price which existed at the time ? It proves nothing of the kind. I tell the hon. gentleman that you could not go into the market in the months of October, September, August, or July last, and make a contract for the delivery of rails at the time specified in this contract at any less price than the price we made it for. And you cannot go into the market to-day, if my information is correct, and make a contract for the delivery of rails within six, nine or twelve months-
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite wrong in that statement.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) know ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes.

Then I will have to yield to his superior knowledge. I am speaking from my information. I do know that when we made this contract for these rails we were not agreeing to pay an exorbitant price. I do know that the enormous demands that were being made at that time upon the rail manufacturers made it impossible to get

an early delivery at a less cost than that *which is named here. Now, so much for this year. We are not bound as to what the price will be next year. When we come to settle up for the next year's supply of rails, if the contract which has been entered into is carried out and the rails are delivered, we will have to ascertain what the market price is in England and the market price in England is a safe guide. If you go by that you are not paying an exorbitant figure, and we have this company under obligation to accept from us the price which rules in the English market. If they do not agree to furnish us with rails at the price which rules in the English market, we stipulated in making our contract that we were not under any obligation whatever to take the rails from them; that if they have not fulfilled their contract we are under no obligation to fulfil ours. That is a perfectly safe arrangement. I do not know how it would be possible to hit upon any terms which are to have reference at all to the future which would secure or guarantee the exchequer of this country against any loss, against any imposition in price, other than the terms in which that contract has been framed, and when it stipulates that we shall go to the open market in England to find bow much it would be just and fair to pay them for rails we make a stipulation which I do not think anybody can say is not an ample protection to the exchequer of this country.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There are two features of it that attract our attention at the present time. The first is the unwisdom of entering into such a large contract without parliament being consulted. All this is wrong and hon. members on the other side of the House for years and years invariably declared that it was wrong and condemned the previous government for doing that kind of thing to an extent which they thought was not justifiable. Now, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) says that there is nothing wrong in it. It seems to me to be practically another Yukon job-a worse job, some say than the Yukon job. It is, at all events, on a par with it. The same principle is involved. It is dealing with the money belonging to the country in a high handed way which is not, in my opinion, justifiable. The next feature of it is that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals did not treat the House with perfect frankness or fairness when he made the statement he did yesterday. What was that statement ? We have entered into a contract with Mr. Clergue for 25,000 tons of rails at $32.50 a ton.

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) pardon me for an interruption because it may avoid the necessity of his stating what he is proceeding to do. If he will look at ' Hansard ' he will see just 861
what I said on the subject. I said that we had no explicit contract for the full five years, that we had only fixed the rate for one year, and that subsequently, if they were prepared to sell us 25,000 tons of rails per year at the price which ruled in the English market, we understood we had an arrangement with them to take that quantity. These are the very words. Is not that really what we have done ?
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS..

speechtext: No, I should say not.

That is what 1 certainly would say we had done. I will read what I did say :
When we had assured ourselves with reference to what would be a reasonable price to pay, we made a contract with this company to deliver 25,000 tons of the quality and standard which we have been placing upon the road, a rail eighty pounds in weight, and we were to pay them $32.50 per ton, the delivery to commence in the first week in August, and to continue at such a rate that we would be able to lay them before the snow fell. They were to be delivered to us in Montreal-that is in the present year. We have no permanent and explicit contract with them for the future, although in their proposal they asked us to give them a contract for a term of five years, and to give them an order for 50,000 tons with which to commence their industry. We finally concluded to give them an order for 25,000 tons, and while we have no explicit contract with them for any term beyond the year in which we are now entering, we have an understanding with them under which, if they furnish us, as they engage to do, with rails of the quality and standard we require, and at the current price in the English market, we are prepared to continue to take our rails from them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is a contract.
That is a contract, is it not 1
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, certainly. That is a contract to buy for five years.
Well, I say that we had no explicit arrangement because the price is entirely indefinite.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No, you have a five years contract with them.
It is just as I stated, is it not 1
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You said it was for one year, and now you say that it is for five years.
You have a contract for five years.

We have an understanding that we are to purchase rails from them providing they are willing and ready and prepared to sell them to us at the market price in England.
[DOT]2727
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Yon are obliged to take them by your contract.
We are not obliged unless they agree to give them to us at the prevailing price in England.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Does the hon. minister say that the contract is ail on one side ? The government have bound themselves to take
25.000	tons a year, but it is not a contract unless the manufacturers like to give them these rails each year. It is a contract on the minister's side, but it is not a contract on Mr. Clergue's side.
Do hon. gentlemen object to taking Canadian rails if the government can get them as cheaply as they can be got in other quarters ?
You will have to vote for it anyway.

I respectfully submit that my statement was absolutely correct that the minister did not treat this House with frankness and fairness. He left the impression on the House that the contract was only for 25,000 tons, whereas it is for
125.000	tons. He has read from ' Hansard ' and his words have supported the statement that I made. He had a signed and sealed contract between the Minister of Railways as representing the government, and Messrs Clergue as representing the contractors. If this is not a binding contract, I do not know what it is. The condition of the contract is that they shall supply 25,000 tons of rails every year after the first year at the current market value. It is a contract all the same. I say it is not treating the House with frankness that the minister should mislead the House into the belief that there was no contract except for 25,000 tons to be delivered the present season. The other feature to which I wish to refer is the time at which the contract was entered into. When was it ? In October at the very time that the writs had been issued and when the elections were on. I do not know what the date of the contract was.
The 9th of October.

The elections took place on the 7th of November. The contract was entered into at the very time that the writs had been issued and when the elections were on. About the same time he entered into a contract for nineteen locomotives at Kingston, when he telegraphed to his friend there regarding it, so that it might do the greatest amount of good to the party in power at that time. This has explained to me what would seem inexplicable before. I found that the Messrs. Clergue were very active agents in the interests of the present government during the election.
In your county.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
They were making themselves very active in our part of the country. They were writing most diplomatic letters that had a political purpose, and when I wrote to them inquiring if there was truth in the report that this was done for election purposes, they did not deign to answer until about five weeks ago, because they did not dare to do it without having to confess. Now we have the explanation of the whole thing. They were playing into the hands of the Hon. Wm. Mulock, who was directing the campaign in that part of the country. Now we see the nigger in the fence. This contract comes out. A day ago, the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) told us that the contract was for
25,000	tons of rails, but he admits to-day that it is for 125,000 tons, and he merits the condemnation and censure of this House for not treating us with fairness. The minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) bought these rails in the face of a falling market. It must have been known to him that the price of steel was going down at the time he made this contract.
Not at that time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, it was going down at that time. And to-day, only a few months after he made this contract, he is forced to admit that the price is $6 a ton less than this contract price. The whole thing looks like a scaly transaction, and the public of Canada will condemn it and condemn the minister. It is a contract that should receive the condemnation of this House and of the country.

There is an old saying about teaching your grandmother how to suck eggs, and here we have the Liberal government professing to teach the Conservative party to set up an industry in this country. In fact the Minister of Railways has delivered us a lecture on the subject. Well, We do want an iron industry in Canada, and the government should encourage it, but they should go the right way about encouraging it. In this case they have gone back on all their record In the past; they have started out to build up an iron industry now, a thing which they told us in the past was an impossibility in this country. Why did they not invite capitalists to confer with them and discover from whom they could receive the best terms. That was not their policy at all. But just when an election is at hand they make a secret contract about which the public know nothing until four months after the elections are over. The whole transaction has not a good look about it; and especially so when we remember that these very men have heretofore been opposed to

the encouragement of an iron industry in Canada. They told us it was a hot-house industry, and that you could only encourage it by bounties and prohibitive duties, but now they go back on all their professions In this respect. What does the hon. member for South Oxford (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) say now about encouraging this hot-house industry ? In speech after speech, year after year, he has declaimed against encouraging any iron industry in Canada. What has he got to say now ? What has he to say to his colleagues in the government professing to teach the people of Canada to-day how a steel industry is to be encouraged here ? They make a secret contract and that in itself is opposed to all their declarations in the past. They should have intimated to the rail-makers of the United States and of Great Britain and of Europe that they were disposed to encourage the production of steel rails in Canada, and that they were prepared to make a contract with the company that would establish that industry on the best terms. But they make a secret arrangement which they are ashamed of now, and which the people of the country from one end to the other will repudiate. What becomes of their old idea of having public competition for all these things ? Why, Sir, with the bounties and one thing and another the people of Canada will have to pay $40 a ton for these rails.
What has the bounty got to do with it ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The people have to pay the bounty.
You will have to pay the bounty anyway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is begging the question. The people of the country will pay in round figures $40 a ton for these rails, and as to the price of rails In the market to-day I read the following extract from the New York World of yesterday :
Mr. Charles Thullin, a Pennsylvania contractor, recently secured a contract to supply rails for Russia's great Siberian Railway. He asked the leading steel trust companies here for bids. They all asked him about $35 per ton, with freight to be added.
How does that strike you ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Wait a minute.
Mr. Thullin went over to England, sub-let his contract to an English firm, and one of the same companies that had asked him $35 plus freight here, sold the rails at $24 a ton, delivered in England to the English sub-contractors.
That is the ruling price to-day : $24 a ton for these rails, rolled in America and delivered in England.
That is the ruling price, is it ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That is the price quoted in the New York World of yesterday for these rails for the Siberian Railway delivered in England, and it is $24 a ton. As my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) has pointed out, this contract was made with Mr. Clergue in the face of a falling market. A man in the position of the Minister of Railways must have prevision, and the government must have prevision and they must have known that the market for steel was declining. Every one knows that the price of iron had got to the highest point about a year ago, and that there was bound to be a decline, tout in the face of that the government made this contract. I say that the contract is a bad one, because it was made in view of a falling market. I say that the contract is a bad one even on the ground of encouraging a native industry, because the government did not go the right way about it by putting it up to competition. I say that the contract is a bad one, because it was made in secret, and I say that a grievous wrong has been perpetrated on the country by the government in entering into such a contract. We have heard something about there being nickel in these rails. Is nickel an essential part of the rail, or will Mr. Clergue say hereafter : I am willing to abide by the price in England; but what is the price in England for rails containing two or three per cent of nickel ? That price may be $30 or $40 a ton in England, because they cannot make nickel rails in England, and thus we may have to pay an exorbitant price under this contract. Surely the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) cannot justify this. The minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) tried to make the House believe that this was not a five years contract, but from what we have heard to-day the period of five years is one of the essences of the contract. True the price may be reduced a year after, but if that idea of nickel being in the rails has any meaning, it undoubtedly may interfere with any reduction in the price. The result of the whole transaction is that this country is committed to a five years contract for rails with Mr. Clergue, and at a price which Mr. Clergue may fix and not the government. That is how it looks to me. What can the people think of this government professing to encourage the steel industry in this country ? Why, they are going back on their record as free traders. Did not we hear the Prime Minister state the other day that he was still a free trader, and did not believe in the encouragement of hothouse industries in Canada. What has he got to say to this transaction 1 The two things do not go together. There is in them what is in nearly every one of their propositions, a great deal of hypocrisy. They are hypocrites in regard to taxation,

in regard to expenditures for public works, in regard to the encouragement of native industries ; and it will be as political hypo crites that they will be tried by the people of this country. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) smiles ; what does he think of this transaction ? We all remember the steel rail scandal in the time of the Mackenzie government ; but, it was as nothing compared with this. Steel rail scandals run in the blood of hon. gentlemen opposite ; this one comes out in the second generation. This great steel combine in the United States may collapse ; it may not be able to overtake English, Belgian and German competition ; and steel rails may before long rule at $20 a ton. True, they may go up ; but, no minister can justify what the hon. gentleman has tried to justify to-day-the making of that contract for five years in view of a falling market. No. he made it in view of an election on the 7th of November last.

It is difficult to satisfy hon. gentlemen opposite. To-day it suits their purpose to complain that the government lias not gone to the United States when it desires to procure additional rails. If it were a case of cars and locomotives, such as have recently been purchased by the government for the Intercolonial Railway, and the hon. gentleman were to repeat what he has stated in this House, and what other gentlemen beside him have stated year after year, he would say that it was a crying wrong for this government to have gone to the United States and asked American manufacturers to tender. It was used as an election cry from one end of Canada to the other by hon. gentlemen opposite and their newspaper jiress, that we did not get our locomotives in Canada, but had got most of them in the United States. I would like to know what we can possibly do to satisfy these hon. gentlemen. We felt that every interest called upon us to encourage the building of locomotives in Canada. We took hold of the matter, knowing that gentlemen of capital were willing to revive the Kingston industry, gave them a contract, and encouraged them to put their money into the enterprise of constructing locomotives in Canada. We have done the same with regard to rails.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Are you supplying the money ?
So far as the purchase price of the article made for us is concerned, yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Are you supplying the money for the locomotives made in Kingston in advance of delivery ?

We are furnishing the manufacturers of the locomotives at Kingston with Mr. MACLEAN.
payments on account as the work progresses.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Hear, hear.
Certainly we are ; we are not ashamed of it; we glory in it, if you want to know, because it is giving employment to 500 or 600 men in the city of Kingston.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

Let the heathen rage-we stand on our record ; and we put the rail question on the same footing as we put the engine question. They stand together, and they will be both defensible, in the good opinion and the judgment of this country.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would the minister allow me to ask him a question in regard to that ? Why did he not do that before, instead of sending orders for twenty locomotives to the United States ?

I thank the hon. gentleman for asking me the question. We did it the moment an appeal was made to us to do it. We did not do it before, because we had given to the Kingston works, while they were in operation, orders for the building of every locomotive they would undertake to build ; and we did not go to the United States for an engine until they failed us. They had contracts for the manufacture of engines for the Intercolonial Railway unfinished when they closed their doors. Yet, hon. gentlemen opposite, from one end of Canada to the other, denounced the conduct of the Minister of Railways and the government because we did, when necessity compelled us, go outside of Canada and get locomotives from the neighbouring country. But, Sir, men came to us who, we were satisfied, had an interest in the country, and who desired to re-establish those works, from a public point of view as well as from a business point of view ; and they said, we will get the capital, put it in, and give employment to 500 or 600 people at least to commence with, if you will give us an order so that we can get the undertaking on its feet. As soon as they agreed to do that, we ceased to give orders for locomotives to the United States. We hope we shall be in a position, when these works are under way at Sault Ste. Marie, to do the same thing with regard to the production of rails.' The establishment of a steel rail industry means a great deal for Canada. The amount of money going out of Canada for rails would be greatly augmented with the increased construction of railways in the future. A very large drain is made on the resources of Canada; and when Mr. Clergue came to us and made such a proposition as he did in June last, knowing him to be an enterprising man, knowing the character of the work he had achieved, and
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: the immense number of people to whom he was giving employment, we felt that he was entitled to a hearing- -
And a contract.

And we gave him a hearing on business grounds ; and I want to say to my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maeleau) that we did not contract to buy upon a falling market. We ascertained what the price of rails was then. There were some people who thought that after a lapse of time, possibly before many months, the price of rails might fall ; but, there was then no evidence of it, and there was a great body of opinion to the effect that the price of rails would continue to rise.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Wa s not the price of
steel going down all the time last year ?

No, Sir, I say it was not ; and 1 defy the hon. gentleman to prove that it was. I can bring the names of persons who bought rails after we made this contract, and who agreed to pay a higher price than we agreed to pay.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Who purchased at a higher price ?

I think I can give the hon. gentleman the statement ; I am going to ascertain. We did not buy in a falling market. The hon. gentleman takes out his New York paper, and absolutely ignoring the very language and pith of the statement he reads, says it shows that rails can be bought in the open market at $24 per ton. But, what he did read shows that the price which the makers of rails asked is $35 per ton.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The combine price.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And the hon. gentleman bought at the combine price.

I did not, unless all the rail producers throughout the world are selling at combine prices. I bought at a price which I was satisfied was the market price ruling in England. Is that a combine market ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes.

If the whole world is in a combine, and you have to buy rails at all, then you have to buy them from'a combine market. If what the hon. gentleman says is true, I do not see how you can avoid buying in a combine market. The hon. gentleman says that $35 is the price that was asked, and that since rails have gone down, and we can buy them at $24. We find from this
statement read by the hon. gentleman that $35 was the price asked by tne rail manufacturers when called upon to name the figures they wanted; but later on, when they found that these rails were going to England, they agreed to lower the price in order to be able to supply the English market. Is the hon. gentleman not aware that that is a common practice among manufacturers and not confined to manufacturers of the United States alone ? There may be manufacturers in this country who do the same thing, and it is a practice which is very common among manufacturers in the United States.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why did the hon. gentleman not avail himself of this practice and get the rails at reduced prices ?

Why then does the hon. gentleman denounce the Minister of Railways and Canals for doing with respect to locomotives what he has the temerity to call on him to do with respect to rails ? If he can condemn us in the one case for doing a certain thing, how can he condemn us in the other case for not doing it ? The hon. gentleman is riding a pair of horses, each of which is going in a totally different direction from the other. You could not establish the industry in Canada if you went to the manufacturers of rails in the United States and said to them : We want to get quotations from you for rails to be shipped to Canada in competition with rails that may be purchased from other sources. How quickly would they not, in that case, drop [DOT] their prices from the figures they would ask if we simply went to them and asked their quotations. The hon. gentleman is denouncing us for not having done the very thing which, under their national policy, they have always contended against our doing. Prior to the adoption of the national policy, they were continually asserting that the manufacturers of the United States were being permitted to make a slaughter market of Canada, and yet to-day because we have adopted a course with respect to the manufacturers of rails, which is calculated to establish the industry in Canada, and prevent the making of this country a slaughter market, they say that we are doing wrong. The present attitude of these hon. gentlemen is entirely inconsistent with the platform on which for years they have been standing. I leave my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) to reconcile, if he can, the statement he himself read with the inference he drew from it. It will be absolutely impossible-
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: My statement which I read shows that the Russian government are getting rails for their railway at $24 and we are paying $32, plus the bonus, or about $40 per ton. I cannot reconcile the hon. gentleman's course with the facts.
If he cannot, I am not going to undertake to do it for him. We have agreed to take these rails for the current year at this price.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And for the succeeding four years.
We have not agreed for more than one year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is not the contract signed ?
It does not fix the price at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No, hut it does the number of tons you must take yearly.
Certainly, we will take for the other four years 25,000 tons yearly, but have not fixed the price. We will take the rails at the current market rate in England.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Is there any period fixed during the year for naming the price ? The manufacturer will no doubt tender each year his supply of 25,000 tons of rails at that particular period of the year when the prices are highest. It seems to me that the government are bound to take the rails at the price ruling at that particular period of the year which is most favourable to the seller.
gentleman tells us about market prices during the past year. If his statement about market prices is not more correct than was his statement yesterday about this contract, I do not think the House would be inclined to place much reliance on it. Here is what the hon. gentleman said about this contract yesterday.
I said at the same time that I would bring the contract down, and if the contract is any more explicit than was my statement, made from recollection, the contract is here and speaks for itself.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman comes down here with estimates and undertakes to give the House certain information. The House is entitled to rely on that information. If he cannot trust to his recollection, he should have the contract in his hands ; he should not make statements that are not justified by the contract when brought down. He has persisted in stating that his remarks with regard to the contract were correct
In effect correct.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: They are not in effect the same.
That is the hon. gentleman's view.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: At whatever date we require these rails to be delivered we will expect to have them, and will have to allow the company reasonable time in which to manufacture them. The price will be that which will rule in England at that time. We will determine upon what is a reasonable and proper time, under the circumstances, to allow for the manufacture of the rails, and then can insist that the price shall be fixed. If the other party is not prepared to agree to the price at that time and make a regular contract with us, then he is not prepared to carry out his agreement.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is nothing in the contract to cover what the hon, minister has just stated, namely, that he can fix the price himself.
It must be implied that the price is to be fixed in advance and according to the market rates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am sure we are glad that one use at least has been found by hon. gentlemen opposite for the national policy, and that is to justify a contract for five years for 125,000 tons of steel rails, not submitted to parliament, and which contract, when it is mentioned in parliament by the hon. gentleman, is not stated very accurately, to put it very mildly. The hon.

And I think I can persuade the hon. minister, if he is capable of persuasion, that that should be his view also. This is what he said :
We have no permanent and explicit contract with them for the future, although in their proposal they asked us to give them a contract for a term of five years, anti to give them an order for 50,000 tons with which to commence their industry.
That is pretty explicit. But the hon. gentleman was not satisfied with that. He went on :
We finally concluded to give them an order for 25,000 tons, and while we have no explicit contract with them for any term beyond the year in which we are now entering, we have an understanding with them under which, if they furnish us, as they engage to do, with rails of the quality and standard we require, and at the current price in the English market, we are prepared to continue to take our rails frcm them.
No one would suppose, having regard to what the hon. gentleman stated, that there was an actual contract under which the government Is bound to take 25,000 tons a year for five years from this very company. But the hon. minister will not dispute that now. He does not dispute it.
If they furnish tuem we are bound to take them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then, is that not a contract ? The only difference between the contract for the present year and that for the ensuing four years is that in one case the price is fixed at $32.60 a ton, and that in the other place the price depends on a question of fact which is capable of being ascertained. The contract is, therefore, just as certain a contract, just as valid and just as binding with respect to the other four years as with respect to the first.
Not as explicit.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not know what the hon. gentleman means by ' explicit.' He said he had no permanent contract with them. But he has brought down a contract covering a term of five years which is just as much a contract for the whole five years as it is for the first year, notwithstanding the difference as to fixing the price to which I have referred. That I may not be accused of speaking without the book, I will read the first paragraph :
'That Her Majesty will In each year during the years 1901 and 1905, both inclusive, purchase from the company and take delivery of 25,000 tons of 2,240 pounds to the ton of first quality steel rails, eighty pounds to the yard, of section from time to time described and approved by the said minister.
There is a distinct engagement.
What is the date of that contract ?

The date does not appear here, but it purports to have been made under an order in council of Oth October, 1000. The other part, as to the engagement of the company to furnish the rails, is found in the last paragraph :
That the company will execute all such contracts as may, during the period of said five years, be drawn in accordance herewith or presented by the minister for execution, and will manufacture and deliver the said rails for the said prices, and in all respects will comply with the provisions of the said contracts or any of them.
Surely, the hon. gentleman should not have come to this House and told us, as he did yesterday, that there was no contract for a term of five years, but a contract for one year with an understanding-an indefinite understanding apparently-as to the remaining four years. But I would like to know why the hon. gentleman found it necessary at that particular time to enter into a contract for a term of five years. He talks about encouraging the industries of Canada. Well, we are all very glad indeed to see that the hon. gentleman Is converted to the view that the industries of Canada should be protected and encouraged, that he has become a believer in the national policy which some of his colleagues, in days gone by, have denounced in such scathing terms.
The time referred to by the hon. gentleman is the time when he himself entertained different views.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not know that the hon. gentleman need have very much to say about that. Perhaps he will inquire of his colleague (Hon. Mr. Fielding) who sits beside him if he holds the same view with regard to secession that he held in 1886.
The House knows all about that. It has heard about it before.

I did not desire to refer to that, and would not have done so had not the hon. gentleman's colleague brought it forward. But I am ready to discuss the matter with the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals or the hon. Minister of Finance at any time and under any circumstances.
I have no objection.
But the Minister of Railways and Canals is not doing his colleague any credit when he introduces that subject in the House.
Don't mind me.

I do not mind the hon. gentleman. I desire to spare his feelings, but his colleague would not permit me to do so. Now, what was the particular necessity for making a contract for five years with this particular company ? Does not the Minister of Railways and Canals know that there are other companies in Canada that propose to develop the steel and iron business ? Does he not know that there is a company in my own province which proposes to engage in the
Never heard of it until long after this.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Indeed ? Then the hon. gentleman is very much behind the times apparently. Because I think it was understood last autumn that that company was about to engage in this business. At all events, the hon. gentleman knew that they were engaging very extensively in the iron and steel business, that their works in that respect are much beyond the works of Mr. Clergue now, that at the present time they are manufacturing iron and sending it to England, and that they are in a better position, probably, to-day to advance the business of manufacturing steel rails than is Mr. Clergue. I do not wish to say a word against that gentleman. I admire his enterprise and hope his undertakings will succeed. I am not criticising Mr. Clergue but the Minister of Railways and Canals

when I say that it might have been preferable for the minister not to make a contract for more than one or two years at the outside and to look to the future to develop industries of this kind not only in this section but in other sections of the country, industries that will have an equal right to consideration at the hands of the government. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) said that this was something like the Yukon contract. But he was hardly just to the Yukon contract. The minister in charge of that had the grace to . insert in that contract the provision that it should not come into effect until confirmed by parliament. But the Minister of Railways and Canals has no scruples of that kind. He comes to parliament with the contract ready made, telling us that parliament has nothing to say about it, binding the country for five years. And the administration of which he is a member has cancelled contracts for the supply of cloth on the ground that the late administration had no right to make a contract beyond the year for which the vote of parliament had been passed. I know of one case in my own province, and there are many other cases I believe in which that was the policy of the administration with respect to such matters. Having cancelled contracts on that ground, a member of this same administration comes to this parliament with a contract for five years, and [ does not even tell parliament correctly what the terms of it are. And we should never have known what the terms were, had it I not been for my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) who asked that the contract should be laid on the Table before this rote was proceeded with. I do think the Minister of Railways and Canals has not shown very much pro- i vidence or very much judgment in entering into this contract. He tells us that the price of steel rails was not falling during the past year. But, as a business man, he had every reason to believe that the price would probably fall this year. As a matter of fact, according to his own statement, this country is losing not less than from $150,000 to $200,000 a year on this very contract; 25,000 tons of these steel rails are to be provided during the present year, and on these rails, taking the statement of the Minister of Railways and Canals himself, we will lose no less a sum than $150,000. Now, we may or may not lose to a corresponding amount in future years ; possibly with regard to those, the price is fixed on a better basis, although it may be as the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals has pointed out, that you cannot get a basis on the English market which will do justice to this contract, because, although it is not stated in the contract, nevertheless it is stated in the speech of the minister, that these rails are to contain nickel, and the minister has left it open Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
in the second clause of this contract to make a provision that these rails shall contain nickel. In order that I may not be accused of misrepresenting the hon. gentleman, the second clause of the contract is as follows
That the minister shall, on behalf of Her Majesty, each year during the said five years, enter into a contract with the company, specifying, in greater detail than herein set forth, the time and place of the delivery of such rails, the section approved, the price and mode of payment, with other incidental particulars and provisions, at the discretion of the minister.
Now, that leaves a very wide door open for the minister to deal with this matter during the next five years. I think the contract is for that reason open to the criticism which has been made upon it by my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart).

I want to reply to the emphatic contradiction the Minister of Railways and Canals made to my statement that the contract was made in the face of a falling market. He said : I deny that it is a fact, and I challenge him to prove it. I have the proof in my hand. I take the Monthly Summary of the Commerce and Finances of the United States for January, 1901. Remember that the recommendation was made to council regarding this transaction on the 2Gth of September, and on the 9th of October it was passed. Now, what was the market price then? On the 26th of September steel rails were quoted at $35 a ton.
That is $2.40 more than the contract price.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: On the 3rd of September they were quoted at $35 a ton ; on the 10th of September they were quoted at $30 a ton, having fallen $5 ; on the 30th of September they were quoted at $30, and on the I 3rd of October they were quoted at $26. Therefore, I was right in my statement that the contract was made in the face of a falling market, as the price fell from $35 on the 3rd of September down to $26 about the time he entered into the contract. Does that not look like a shady transaction of a political character ? This is the official record of the markets during the whole year. Now, when the Minister of Railways and Canals gets up and emphatically contradicts a statement as he did, I would like some better authority to stand by than his own words.

With regard to the alleged readiness of the works in Cape Breton to supply these rails, I think I am correct in saying that the promoters of that enterprise have never made any proposal to the government for making rails, and I think I am also correct in stating that they have not been in a position to offer any rails up to the present time. I think they are

now contemplating an enlargement of tlieir operations with a view to making rails ; but it is correct to say that up to the present time the promoters of that enterprise have not been ready to make rails, they have made no proposal to make rails, and therefore the two companies have not come into competition. I hope to learn that by the enlargement of their operations they will be able to make rails, and if they do, I have no doubt that we shall find a chance to give them an order on fair and reasonable terms.

I think from what I saw in the public press that the additional bonds placed upon the market by that company in December last were, among other things, intended for the purpose of enlarging their plant so that they could make steel rails. Of course, the hon. gentleman is better informed than I am with regard to that, and I will accept his word ; but that is my recollection of what I saw.
The only point, perhaps, in which I am better informed than my hon. friend is in the fact that they have made no proposal to this government to supply rails.
I did not suppose they had.

But the hon. gentleman mentioned the two enterprises as coming into conflict. I think the Cape Breton people are now contemplating the manufacture of rails, but the hon. gentleman referred to them as if they were to be considered in any contract for rails. My recollection is that the additional bonds, to which the hon. gentleman referred, were issued only a few days ago.

Before the House' takes recess, I want to say one word in reply to the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule). I tlmnk him for the extreme courtesy with which he has referred to my statement on the subject. But I desire to state to this committee now that nothing, in my opinion, could be more unfair, nothing could be more unjust than the hon. gentleman's statement, and the hon. gentleman's method of giving support to that statement. The hon. gentleman knows that the whole basis of this arrangement between the government and the Sault Ste. Marie Company was the state of the open market in England. Why was the open market in England chosen ? It was chosen because no sane man would make any agreement to bind himself to the momentary fluctuations of the rail market in the United States, which is up to-day and down to-morrow, at the arbitrary wink and demand of the combine which controls the output. It is unfair for the hon. gentleman to challenge the correctness of my statement when I said that we did not buy upon a falling market, or, in other words, that
there was no fall below the price we had fixed, by showing that the iron proprietors in the United States had lowered the price of rails from $35 down to $26 within a certain period. Let the hon. gentleman search the records and he will find that the price goes up and down, up and down again ; it is pulled up and dropped down to suit the fancy of these people, and is not the result of fair business operations. Upon the open market in England no such condition of things, he will find, obtains. I would like the hon. gentleman to pursue his inquiries further, and to see whether the quotations were as variable in the English market as they were in the United States market, according to what he has read. I made inquiries from some friends in Montreal, I will not say on the 9th of October, but on the 26th of September, and thereabouts, a few days before, when we were coming to a conclusion upon this matter. I inquired from friends in Montreal what the English prices were, and I found they were maintaining about the same standard as the price at which rails were offered to us some months previously. Therefore, I felt justified, and the government felt justified, in deciding that we would give to Mr. Clergue's company the same price that we were then paying for rails. Now, I ask the hon. gentleman to turn up the English quotations. While I did not have the English quotations before me, I did have statements from people that I believed knew, who were reliable, as to what the price of rails was. Now let me make one further remark. The hon. gentleman says we bought on a falling market. Supposing we had bought on a market that fell-and no doubt the market has fallen in a sense-can you avoid that? Can. any prescience foresee a falling market so as to provide against it ? No. The hon. gentleman nods his head. I say no. You have to make your bargain for some time ahead. What time do you choose ? When you want to ensure the earliest possible delivery. ' We had to make our arrangement with them in order to ensure delivery during this present season. We could not tell; the price might go up. You have to take them when you can get them. You must take the price as it exists when you make your contract unless there is some good reason for believing that a lower price may prevail. The year before that we wanted to buy 10,000 tons of rails. We went into the market. We had to give some months' time for delivery-I cannot say how many months elapsed before these rails were delivered-previously when we made our contract. But, we made our contract at the best price we could obtain. We made it for $20 a ton and before half the time had elapsed for delivery we could have sold those rails for from $34 to $35 a ton, $14 or $15 advance on the price that we had paid. No human foresight can always pro-

vide against falls or rises in the price. Make the best arrangement you can bona fide and in the exercise of reasonable judgment and let the consequences follow. That is^ what we are doing to-day in this case. We made a good many thousands of dollars by buying the year before. It may be that if we had the foresight to enable us to know that there would be a fall in the price, if we had had reason to suppose that rails could be got for summer delivery at a lower price, we might have possibly saved a few dollars in the present transaction. These are the circumstances under which the arrangement was made. It was made fairly, squarely and bona fide. It was made, Ij have no hesitation in saying, with the desire to encourage the establishment of an enterprise which we had no expectation would be established otherwise. It was made at the price then governing and at a price which is fair to the public.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to move an amendment to the motion which is in your hands, an amendment of which notice was given some time ago. The subject-matter of the amendment has been discussed at considerable length both in the Railway Committee and before the Committee of the Whole House, and I do not intend to take up the time of the House, but merely to ask for a division on the motion. I move, seconded by Mr. Maclean :
That Bill No. 13 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee for the purpose of amending it by adding the following section :-
' His Majesty shall have the right at any time to take over the undertaking, property rights and franchises of the company, and for that purpose the provisions of the Expropriation Act shall apply.
From any valuation placed upon such property so taken there shall be deducted, on payment, the amount of any bonus or subsidy paid by the government of Canada to the company towards the construction of such line of railway or any part thereof.'
ill'. R. L. BORDEN (Halifax). Mr. Speaker, before the question is put, I would like to say a few words. This amendment has already been discussed to some extent Mr. BLAIR.
when the Bill was in committee. With the first part of it I am heartily in accord, but with the second part I am not in accord for reasons that I have already stated in the committee. It does not seem to me that it would be an equitable thing in all cases to deduct the whole amount of the subsidy. 1 would suggest to the hon. mover of the amendment (Mr. Clarke) that it would be fairer to the company if the latter part of the resolution read in this way :
From any valuation placed upon such property so taken there shall be deducted, on payment, a reasonable amount in respect of any bonus or subsidy

And so forth. Instead of deducting the whole amount of the bonus or subsidy, which might not be equitable in some cases where the value of the property was very much less than the amount it had cost, you should take a reasonable amount of such bonus or subsidy, leaving it to the tribunal which fixes the value to determine what such reasonable amount should be.

subtopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: If it is in order to accept the "suggestion made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Borden), I will be very glad to do it.
