subtopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
Before the motion is put, I would like to call the attention of the House to the fact that the proposal in the motion goes further than I think it should. For instance, the resolution says that if the government desires to obtain control of this national railway from the Georgian Bay to Lake Ontario :
-they shall have the right to take over the undertakings, property rights and franchises of the company, and for that purpose the provisions of the Expropriation Act shall apply.
Now, this company have its terminals and warehouse at Fort William or Duluth or Milwaukee, or Chicago, and they may have warehouses in all of these places.	IVhat
right would the government of Canada have to take over such properties ? What business would the government of Canada have to take over these four steamers that they propose in their minds to have on the upper lakes, and the half dozen steamers they talk about on Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence ? Would Canada undertake to run a steamboat business ?

subtopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
Certainly not. We do not desire to do it, and we will not do it. They insist that if we take over the railway we would also have to take over these other properties, and it simply means that if they do not have complete control over the railway they do not want the steamboats at all. If the government acquires the railway it will be so much capital of the company liberated, and the money for the railway will be handed back to the company, less the amount of bonuses they received. That means that the actual amount of money they have expended on the railway will be paid back to them. The plain English of the contention of this company is, that if they have the steamers they must have the railway, and it is because the ownership of the railway would give their steamers an advantage over all other steamers carrying freight on the upper lakes and across this railway, and down the St. Lawrence to the sea, that they want the railway. The railway does not disappear if they retain the steamers. A railway owned by the government would be as eligible to carry the products from these steamers on the upper lakes on to the sea as would this private railway, and indeed it would be more advantageous for them, because past experience tells us that a government railway will carry products cheaper than any private railway. They would, therefore, be in a better position with these steamers on the upper and lower lakes than they would be to-day if they owned both the steamers and the railway. I contend that we should not take power-which, I suppose, means that it would be binding on us-to take over the railway and the steamers and the warehouses in the United States and in Canada. Let them go on with their steamer business, and the government of Canada will give them all the facilities they give any other carrier. Our experience on the Intercolonial Railway is, that goods are carried at about cost, and no doubt if the government owned this road the same thing would occur in this case. I am in favour of the principle of this resolution, but I would like to see that part of it which I object to eliminated. Of course, I would vote for the resolution sooner than not have the principle incorporated in the Bill at all, but, I would infinitely prefer to have that part of the resolution left out. This road is ostensibly a portion of the through traffic route of the country, just as the Welland canal is a link in the system of communication from the great North-west to the sea. It would, of course, be disastrous if the control of the Welland canal passed into the hands of a private corporation, who could charge what tolls they pleased, and who could put onerous restrictions on commerce. Our experience is, that the government never interfere in a case of that kind, and I cannot help stating that if this road is a necessity, the parliament of Canada, and the people of Canada, should be the owners of it. It looks to me, on the face of it, that this charter is a kind of speculation. There are a number of lines now connecting the Georgian Bay with Lake Ontario. There is the Northern Railway from Collingwood through Meaford to Toronto ; the Canadian Pacific Railway from Owen Sound to Toronto ; the Grand Trunk Railway, from Wiarton down through the country to Hamilton, and other points on Lake Ontario, and from Owen Sound as well. There is the Midland system from Midland to Belleville or Port Hope, or any of these ports on the lake, so that, in view of all the existing lines, this is, to my mind, a railway which should not get a government subsidy. The Minister of Railways has declared already his opinion that there should be no subsidy granted by the parliament of Canada for this road, and I am pleased to hear that, because it agrees with my own opinion. If this line is a necessity for the commerce of the country, then the government should make it a link in the canal system direct, instead of going at it in the roundabout way that this resolution proposes. However, parliament has disposed of that. Last session the House of Commons declared In favour of granting this charter, but the Senate, in its wisdom, declared that the people of the country had the most interest in it, and that the charter which was then asked for by the city of Toronto, the board of trade, and the commercial men of the country, should also receive consideration. I do not think there should be put into this Bill a provision that the government will be obliged to purchase those steamers, warehouses, elevators and terminals at

places in the states or in Canada ; because the governemut of Canada would have no use for them, but this company would have the same use for them, and a better use, with more opportunity of doing business, if they desired to do it fairly if the government owned that connecting link than they would have if it were owned by a private company. If it is owned by a private company and the steamers are owned by a private company, they will be able to control the traffic of the road to the detriment of common carriers, and I do not think you could make an enactment of this parliament that would prevent them having the advantages of that control. I think it would be disastrous to this country if that were permitted ; and as this resolution goes in the right direction, though it goes a little further than I would approve of, I will give it my support.

speechtext: I am rather amused to hear the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) talk absolutely against the amendment of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), and then say he intends to support it. speechtext: If I may be allowed to set the hon. gentleman at rest in that matter, 1 will say that there is absolutely no truth in it.

speechtext: No antagonism ? I am ready to accept the hon. gentleman's statement. The newspapers have always said so, however, and the indications point in that direction. The amendment of the hon, member for West Toronto is to my mind in the nature of an absurdity. The hon. member for West York has very truly outlined the situation, as to what would happen in the event of this amendment carrying-that the government would be bound to take over all the boats, all the terminals, all the plant which this company may see fit to institute in the carrying out of its scheme.

subtopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext: That is the proposal of the Minister of Railways.

subtopic: CANADA NATIONAL RAILWAY AND TRANSPORT COMPANY.
speechtext:
It is the proposal of the hon. member for West Toronto. The proposal of the Minister of Railwavs, as I understood it, was to expropriate the railway and nothing more. The hon. member for West Toronto, in the Railway Committee, stated that his resolution ' was to take over everything that this company might inaugurate in carrying out its scheme. The proposition to expropriate the property less the bonus is not, I think, a proper suggestion. If this scheme is carried out to Mr. WALLACE.
its legitimate conclusion, it means the expenditure of a very large amount of money. It means the expenditure of a large amount of money in order to get business. Suppose this company goes on for some years and loses money-loses more money in endeavouring to work up a business than the amount of the bonus would be, if it ever gets a bonus; and it is not yet asking for a bonus. Why should we endeavour to cross the bridge before we reach it ? This company has not yet asked for a bonus. When it does, it is time enough then to make propositions as to what shall be embodied in the Bill granting the bonus. But when you lay down a hard and fast proposition that any mercantile venture shall be expropriated by the government less the bonus that is given to it, I say you are laying down a proposition which is absolutely bad in principle. The gentlemen who are investing their money in the scheme may spend perhaps thousands of dollars more than the bonus amounts to, and when it has come to be a paying business, the government might say :	We will take this over now, after
you have spent the bonus we have given to you, and also spent money out of your own pockets. The hon. leader of the opposition has a view in the right direction, but it does not go far enough. He sees the dawning of the day, he knows what is the proper legislation, but he has not the courage of his opinion; he is a little afraid of his supporters behind him. It the leader of the opposition would do as he believes, I think he would say that this amendment should be voted down. His own suggestion points in that direction-that you cannot fairly take from the value of an article the bonus which has been given to it by the government of Canada, if it is given a bonus at all. If it is not a legitimate transaction, do not give it a bonus; but if it is entitled to a bonus, give it one, and then when you take it over, do not say : You men have made a property which is valuable to the Dominion of Canada, but we will expropriate the property and take away from you the bonus that we have given you, though you have spent perhaps thousands of dollars beyond the bonus in order to make the property valuable.

What was the result of the settlement of the disagreeable trouble that took place over the St. Regis lock-up, and what became of those Indians that were arrested ?	*

Tlie difficulty at the St. Regis reserve to which the hon. gentleman refers is of long standing. The officers of the department, when I first had it called to my attention, informed me that there had been a difficulty for some years owing to the fact that the

American Indians whose reserve adjoins the Canadian reserve were constantly fomenting disaffection amongst our Indians and endeavouring to persuade them that they should not submit to our Indian administration. These Indians made a practice of coming every little while to Ottawa by deputations and demanding changes in the administration which the department did not see its way clear to grant. They had some peculiar idea about the sanctity of their reserve and they had refused to allow provincial constables to go on their reserve to execute writs. Matters were getting into such a state that I made up my mind it was absolutely necessary to make them understand, as gently as possible of course, that the law had to be observed. The matter was brought to a head by a determination that we would appoint a constable to see that the law was enforced, and to make a long story short, we sent down the Dominion chief of police to prevent the constable being obstructed. The Dominion chief of police with some assistants went upon the reserve for the purpose of arresting one of the ringleaders in the riot and two or three of the Indians forced their way into the Indian office, assaulted the chief of police, threatened his life and he finally shot one of the Indians in self-defence. A number of the Indians were brought before the court and after a great deal of negotiation on both sides we finally came to an arrangement whereby the case went by default, and the Indians were let go upon agreement that they would appear for trial when called upon. This is the most difficult case connected with the management of the Indians I have had anything to do with, and it is necessary to use firmness with a good deal of consideration in order to bring about a peaceful result. It is necessary that we should follow up what we have done by having on the reserve a place of such a character that in case of disturbance we can take care of offenders. It is for that purpose we have asked for this vote.

Has the superintendent general of Indian Affairs abandoned the effort on his part to see that the Indians observe the law in the event of trouble. As I understand, the case against the Indians went by default and they were released. It appears to me that the Indians will feel that they are masters of the situation, and if so I do not see what great benefit you' will derive from a lock-up when you cannot enforce the law.

Every step was taken after consultation with those who were best acquainted with the facts of the case. The Solicitor General gave the prosecution his best attention and we allowed the prosecution to go because we were satisfied that the Indians having 871
been taught a sufficient lesson would be amenable to reason and that any further prosecution would result in exasperating them. Those in the neighbourhood strongly pressed me not to take any steps at all because they thought it would exasperate the Indians. Every one who is acquainted with the facts is satisfied we did what was best. I am not going to say that there will be no further trouble. Any one who knows anything about Indian character knows that it is impossible to predict that. But I am satisfied we have done the best that could be done, and that with judicious management we will be able to get along without further trouble.

You are going to build up a lock-up as a kind of object lesson to terrorize them.

The MINISTER OF THE LYrna .wR. It would be difficult for me to give accurate information on that point, because in the different reserves there are a few here and there engaged in agriculture. What success has attended the efforts of the government of late in that line ? And what quantity of grain and other supplies have the Indians raised for themselves ?

Generally, the results of the work during the last three years have been very encouraging. The Indians are rapidly becoming more self-supporting. They have been particularly successful in stock-raising. Where the country is adapted to that pursuit, the Indians manifest a desire to take it up, and, where we have been able to secure an Indian agent who understands the Indian nature, there has been a marked improvement. The amount of grain and other crops raised my hon. friend will find fully set forth in the report of the Department of Indian Affairs. Generally speaking that statement shows that the value of farm products, including hay raised last year on the Indian reserves in the North-west Territories -that does not include Manitoba-was $162,639.07. Upon one of the reserves which I had the pleasure of visiting last summer we have an agent who has been extremely sue-

cessful. The Indians there raised over 10,000 bushels of first-class wheat. They have become extremely prosperous. The agent has been so successful that I have placed him in charge of three reserves, in the hope that he will bring about a similar state of affairs in the other two. The House may rely upon it that great progress has been made. In the organized portion of the country there is no Indian population that may be considered dangerous so far as the peace of the country is concerned. The Indians are becoming rapidly a peaceful population and self-sustaining. The expenditure we are making is very large, but it is made in pur' suance of a policy favoured by parliament for many years based upon a belief that it is better-aside from the justice of the question-to bring the Indians into a state of civilization or comparative civilization, so that they may not be a menace to the country, than to take any chances of their becoming a disturbing factor in the community. Generally the results have been satisfactory. The Indians of Manitoba are differently situated. They are generally what we call wood Indians as distinguished from ' plain Indians, and they follow occupations of a more varied kind. They work in the lumber woods and engage in other occupations, and, from the beginning have been a rather better class of Indians to deal with. They are in a fairly satisfactory state and are making good progress.

In the case of boarding schools there is a fixed amount per capita for each pupil which the school shows to have in attendance. The same thing is true in regard to the industrial schools, only we pay a larger amount for an industrial school than for a boarding Mr. ROCHE (Marquette).
school. In the case of a day school the plan is not invariably followed, but in most cases we pay the salaries of the teachers and maintain the schools ourselves. In some cases we simply contribute the salaries of the teachers and the churches take care of the schools. In Manitoba and the Northwest Territories Indian education is almost entirely carried on through the different churches. The Roman Catholic Church, the Episcopalian Church, the Presbyterian Church and the Methodist Church, are the four churches which take the largest part in the work and the educational institutions are, almost in every case, affiliated with some one of these different churches.
As time goes on and as settlement takes place, and they are taking more and more, year by year, to agriculture, is there any decrease in the expense of keeping up these schools ?	[DOT]

I am bound to say that I cannot observe any decrease. I find continually a disposition to increase these expenses, because there is a continual demand made upon us for more schools and educational operations are extended. I am constantly in the position of having to resist demands for more schools.
We were told some years ago that after a time these schools would be practically self-supporting. Can the minister tell us how much per capita these schools cost V

In the case of boarding schools we pay a uniform rate of $72 per head. The church authorities say they want to establish a boarding school on a reserve, and we say: very good we will allow you $72 each for so many pupils, and they have to show that that number at least attend the school. In many cases'a considerably larger number attend, but they only get a grant for the number agreed upon. For the industrial schools we pay as follows : Rupert's Land school, near Winnipeg, $125 per head, for 120 pupils. St. Boniface school $110 per head for 100 pupils. Brandon school $120 per head for 100 pupils. Qu'Appelle school $125 a head for 225 pupils. Regina school $130 for 125 pupils; Battleford school $150 per head for 120 pupils; Red Deer school $140 per head for 80 pupils. What success has attended the education of the Indians in these schools ? Are they making progress ?[DOT]

That is a matter in connection with which there is a very great difference of opinion.
I have given a good deal of personal attention to the question and my own conclusion, reached about a year ago after con-

suiting with men of experience, is :	That
the money we spend for boarding schools is the most effective, and that we are-getting better results from it than the money we spend for industrial schools. It is the general conclusion of all familiar with Indian education that the ordinary day school is very ineffective, and that wherever a boarding school can be substituted for a day school it is desirable to do so. It is a little more expensive but the work is far more effective. The reason is that when the Indian child comes from the wigwam to school the influences centered upon the child at school are generally effaced by the home associations of the child. The boarding school is 1 think the best. It is not any more effective in regard to each pupil than is the industrial school, but the latter is much more expensive and in my judgment we get better value for our money than in the case of the former. When I took charge I found that the principals of the industrial schools kept the pupils for a length of time which seemed to me to be unreasonable, and I had to issue an order which resulted in a considerable number of pupils being discharged; they having been kept there as long as the state could be expected to keep them. The principals of the schools feared what would happen to the pupils if they left the schools, and of course that was some reflection upon the operation of the system. If a pupil spent five or six years in an industrial school at a cost to the state of $2,000 or $3,000, it was a poor commentary on the system if the pupil had to be kept in school after that for protection. One of the difficulties we have to face is to determine what shall be done with the pupils after they leave the industrial schools. They have then become so far removed from the ordinary Indian that they ought to be in a position to get along as well as an ordinary white man. But experience shows that in very few cases is the Indian boy or girl capable of taking care of himself or herself in contact with the white race. My own view is that the same amount of money spent on a boy or girl in a boarding school would result in training a very much larger number, and would have a better general effect in elevating the whole Indian race. I dealt with this matter at some length in the House a few years ago, and there was considerable discussion on the subject. I said then that while I was inclined to form that opinion I was not sufficiently clear on the subject to condemn an institution which had been founded before I took office, and I had not arrived at the conclusion that they were not doing sufficiently satisfactory work to warrant a radical change in the whole organization. With one exception there has been no industrial institution founded within the last four years. That exception is in British Columbia, where a church society offered to put up the building and incur all the preliminary expenses.
Mr. SPItOULE. That corroborates the information I have had, namely, that the industrial schools are comparatively a failure, and that the money spent in that direction is almost thrown away, because unless the Indians are kept under control after they leave the school they relapse into a condition little better than before they went to school. We have had them long enough on trial to enable us to determine whether they are a success or a failure, and it is important that the Indian Department should consider as to whether it would not be better to change the system.
